claims.assertion: The only off-route segment in the trip is the 23:06–23:12 detour of 2.96 km identified in F3; the rider's claim that the driver 'took a longer way round' is confined to that single segment.

The rider's agreement names the route taken ('via Bedok South Avenue 3'), so the consent covers exactly the 2.96 km segment recorded in F3 and that segment therefore does not constitute a deviation.

The reason given to the rider was building congestion on the East Coast Parkway, and the traffic records show East Coast Parkway at speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) throughout 22:32–23:35, covering the whole deviation window; no incident is recorded near the route (F12).

The billed excess of $4.45 (F4) is exactly 3.2 km at the $1.41/km rate applied to this RydeTAXI meter, and it corresponds to the very segment the rider approved, so no part of it is an unjustified overcharge.

The ride was metered with no surge multiplier (F5) and contains no unpublished add-ons: base $3.90, distance $34.84, time $12.96, waiting $0.00, platform $1.47 in F6 — every component is a published RydeTAXI metered item, so FARE-1 exposes nothing to refund.

The rider's own record shows 0 upheld disputes in 90 days (F14) and the driver's two previously upheld route disputes are historical profile data only; they cannot be used to decide this trip's deviation question, and no evidence here supports a flag_account referral.

weaknesses: The driver's last-minute reroute still cost the rider extra: F1 shows +3.2 km (+15%) and F2 shows +21.4 minutes against the 28-minute estimate, so the rider genuinely paid more than the estimate, and the rider will cite F1/F2 to argue the outcome was unfair regardless of consent.

The traffic support is thin under RD-4: F10 shows only speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) on the East Coast Parkway and F12 records no traffic incident at all near the route, so the rider will argue there was no 'reasonable cause' and that band 4 does not meet RD-4(a); RD-4(b) alone cannot exempt the segment and is expressly left open (gap G3).
The rider will point to the driver's profile (F15: 2 upheld route disputes in 90 days) to argue a pattern, and may press for flag_account under RD-6 even though the profile cannot decide this case.

The metre-structure fee lines in F6 (distance $34.84, time $12.96) mean the extra kilometres did flow into the fare via F4, so the 'quote is fixed' defence available to non-metered services is not available here.

The driver's record shows 4 disputes and 2 upheld route disputes in 90 days (F15), so if any unexempted detour is found the account-review flag under RD-6 is available as a rider-protective action.

weaknesses: C3–C5 concede the core: the rider's own message 'Sure, go ahead' at 23:03 (F8) precedes the only off-route segment (23:06–23:12, F3), so the driver will argue RD-5 exempts the whole 2.96 km segment and the uphold fails.

RD-4 (b)'s speed-band evidence is at least arguable for the driver's 'traffic building up' story — ECP band 4 = 30–39 km/h during 22:32–23:35 (F10, F11) — even though RD-4 (b) alone is not an exemption.

The rider's own profile shows 1 dispute in 90 d, 0 upheld (F14), so the driver may paint the complaint as a pricing grievance rather than a routing violation.

claims.assertion: The only off-route segment in the trip is the 23:06–23:12 detour of 2.96 km identified in F3; the rider's claim that the driver 'took a longer way round' is confined to that single segment.

The driver asked the rider to agree to the reroute before leaving the optimal route: at 23:03 the driver proposed going round via Bedok South Avenue 3 and at 23:03 the rider replied 'Sure, go ahead' — both timestamps precede the segment start of 23:06 in F3, so the rider consented before the deviation.
The rider's agreement names the route taken ('via Bedok South Avenue 3'), so the consent covers exactly the 2.96 km segment recorded in F3 and that segment therefore does not constitute a deviation.

The reason given to the rider was building congestion on the East Coast Parkway, and the traffic records show East Coast Parkway at speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) throughout 22:32–23:35, covering the whole deviation window; no incident is recorded near the route (F12).

The billed excess of $4.45 (F4) is exactly 3.2 km at the $1.41/km rate applied to this RydeTAXI meter, and it corresponds to the very segment the rider approved, so no part of it is an unjustified overcharge.

The ride was metered with no surge multiplier (F5) and contains no unpublished add-ons: base $3.90, distance $34.84, time $12.96, waiting $0.00, platform $1.47 in F6 — every component is a published RydeTAXI metered item, so FARE-1 exposes nothing to refund.

The rider's own record shows 0 upheld disputes in 90 days (F14) and the driver's two previously upheld route disputes are historical profile data only; they cannot be used to decide this trip's deviation question, and no evidence here supports a flag_account referral.

weaknesses: The driver's last-minute reroute still cost the rider extra: F1 shows +3.2 km (+15%) and F2 shows +21.4 minutes against the 28-minute estimate, so the rider genuinely paid more than the estimate, and the rider will cite F1/F2 to argue the outcome was unfair regardless of consent.

The traffic support is thin under RD-4: F10 shows only speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) on the East Coast Parkway and F12 records no traffic incident at all near the route, so the rider will argue there was no 'reasonable cause' and that band 4 does not meet RD-4(a); RD-4(b) alone cannot exempt the segment and is expressly left open (gap G3).
The rider will point to the driver's profile (F15: 2 upheld route disputes in 90 days) to argue a pattern, and may press for flag_account under RD-6 even though the profile cannot decide this case.

The metre-structure fee lines in F6 (distance $34.84, time $12.96) mean the extra kilometres did flow into the fare via F4, so the 'quote is fixed' defence available to non-metered services is not available here.

points.response: Accepted that F3 records one off-route segment of 2.96 km; the rider's complaint is that extra distance entered the metered fare, which F1 (+3.2 km, +15%) and F4 ($4.45 excess distance billed) quantify.
Accepted: the rider's 23:03 agreement (F8) precedes the 23:06 segment start in F3, so under RD-5 consent existed 'before you go'.

This cuts against the driver, not for him: RD-5 exempts only 'that route change's segment', so the consented 2.96 km segment (F3) is exempt but the remaining billed excess — F1's 3.2 km total minus 2.96 km = 0.24 km — is not covered by the consent, and F4 shows the rider was still billed $4.45 (3.2 km × $1.41) instead of at most $4.17 for the 2.96 km consented route.

Band 4 (30–39 km/h) is neither band 1 nor band 2 and F12 records no incident at all near the route, so there is no RD-4(a) exemption and, per RD-4(b), a speed band alone cannot exempt the segment; the driver's congestion reason is unsupported for the ECP stretch replaced by the Bedok South detour (F10, F12).

The arithmetic does not match the consent: $4.45 billed for 3.2 km (F4) versus the 2.96 km actually consented and driven off-route (F3), i.e. the rider overpaid about $0.28 over the $4.17 that the consented segment can support at $1.41/km (F6).
Agreed there was no surge and no unpublished add-on (F5, F6), so FARE-1 leaves nothing to refund beyond the distance item; the rider's claim is confined to the $4.45 excess-distance line (F4).

Accepted that profile data cannot decide the deviation and the rider does not rely on it for the finding under RD-6; the rider's own 0-upheld record (F14) is likewise irrelevant to whether the $4.45 survived the consent.

The metered breakdown the rider quotes (F1, F6) is not itself a deviation finding; RD-2 only yields a refund once an unexempted segment exists under RD-1/RD-5, and the sole segment here was agreed in advance (F7, F8).
Conceded as to the record: there is exactly one off-route segment, 23:06–23:12, 2.96 km with 0.00 km of optimal route (F3), and that single segment is the whole extent of the deviation.
The rider concedes consent existed and before the turn-off; under RD-5 the agreed segment is 'no_action' for that segment, which is the only segment in the case (F3, F7, F8).

RD-4 governs a driver's 'reasonable cause' defence; the driver does not need it because the reroute was passenger-agreed under RD-5, and the ECP speed band 4 at 30–39 km/h across 22:32–23:35 (F10) is consistent with the 'traffic was building up' message the rider accepted (F7).
The rider's own computation leaves only the 0.24 km matching residual, which RD-2 expressly does not refund, so on the rider's own arithmetic nothing is payable.
The $4.17 request assumes the 2.96 km segment is unexempted, but F7/F8 show the rider agreed to that exact route before its 23:06 start (F3), so RD-5 removes the segment from RD-2 entirely.

The $0.28 figure is the difference between the billed excess and a segment the rider already approved; the metre applied the published $1.41/km rate to distance actually driven (F4, F6), and RD-2 refunds nothing for an exempted segment.
Agreed that the bill contains no unpublished add-on — waiting $0.00, one published $1.47 platform fee, no surge (F5, F6) — so FARE-1 exposes no refundable item.

RD-6 only attaches where RD-2 yields a refund or an RD-1 breach is recorded; with the only segment exempted under RD-5 neither trigger exists, and the profile (F15) cannot be used to decide the routing question.
